A.explanation: At $I = 0.36\text{ mA}$ the two p.d.s read from the graph add to $12\text{ V}$, satisfying Kirchhoff's voltage law for the series loop.

B.explanation: At $I = 0.40\text{ mA}$ the sum of the fixed-resistor p.d. and thermistor p.d. is less than $12\text{ V}$, so this current is too large for the $12\text{ V}$ loop.

C.explanation: At $I = 0.48\text{ mA}$ the two components share about $7\text{ V}$ each at the curve crossing, giving a total near $14\text{ V}$, which exceeds the battery e.m.f.

D.explanation: An $I$ of $0.80\text{ mA}$ is the current for the fixed resistor alone across $12\text{ V}$ and ignores the extra p.d. needed by the series thermistor.

hints: Notice the circuit is a single series loop, so the thermistor and fixed resistor must carry the same current $I$ and their p.d.s must add to $12\text{ V}$.
Identify which $I$-$V$ curve is which: the straight line through the origin is the ohmic fixed resistor and the upward-curving line is the non-ohmic thermistor.
Pick a trial current, read $V_{fixed}$ from the straight line and $V_{thermistor}$ from the curve at that same $I$, then adjust $I$ until $V_{fixed} + V_{thermistor} = 12\text{ V}$.
walkthrough: The diagram shows one loop with battery, fixed resistor and thermistor in series, so there is one common current $I$ and, with negligible internal resistance, $V_{fixed} + V_{thermistor} = 12\text{ V}$.
On the $I$-$V$ graph the straight line is the fixed resistor because $I$ is proportional to $V$, while the curved line with increasing gradient is the thermistor.

For any chosen $I$, read horizontally across at that $I$ to find the two $V$ values. For example at $I = 0.40\text{ mA}$, $V_{fixed} \approx 6.0\text{ V}$ from the straight line but $V_{thermistor} \approx 7.0\text{ V}$ from the curve.

Lower the trial current until the sum falls to $12\text{ V}$. At $I = 0.36\text{ mA}$, the straight line gives $V_{fixed} \approx 5.4\text{ V}$ and the curve gives $V_{thermistor} \approx 6.6\text{ V}$.
Then $5.4\text{ V} + 6.6\text{ V} = 12.0\text{ V}$, which matches the battery e.m.f., so the loop current is $0.36\text{ mA}$. This is option A.
